children: Copper prices rose on Wednesday, supported by signs of active demand in top consumer China, though traders remained wary of potential volatility ahead of the U.S. Federal Reserve's interest rate decision.
Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange
gained 0.7% to $14,188 a metric ton by 0947 GMT.
The metal, used in power and construction, is down 5% since hitting a record high of $14,875 last week, as the premium of the COMEX copper futures against London prices (0#LMECMXCU:) fell sharply.
Meanwhile, the Yangshan copper premium (SMM-CUYP-CN), a gauge of Chinese demand for imported copper, rose 7% to $118 per ton, its highest level in almost four years, on Wednesday.
Chinese buyers are taking advantage of the recent price dip to restock copper, helping lift import premiums, said David Wilson, head of metals strategy at BNP Paribas.

Inflows to the U.S. Comex copper stocks slowed down after Reuters reported last week that the White House had yet to decide on refined copper tariffs as officials assess concerns that higher prices could raise manufacturing costs.

LME copper tightness has eased significantly, with spreads moving into contango (CMCU0-3), although that appeared to be driven more by sentiment than by a major increase in available inventory as uncertainty over the U.S. tariffs persists.

In other LME metals, zinc prices were up 0.1% at $3,827, supported by tight inventories outside China, which keep the premium of the LME cash contract over the three-month contract (CMZN0-3) at $124 per ton.
